rezin.name: Rezin
rezin.dateNote: His death is tied to the Assyrian capture of Damascus. His birth year is not known.
rezin.importance: Rezin joins Pekah in a war against Judah. Their attack creates the crisis in which Isaiah gives Ahaz the sign of Immanuel.
rezin.connections: Ally of Pekah. Enemy of Ahaz. Defeated during the expansion of the Assyrian Empire.

ahaz.name: Ahaz
ahaz.dateNote: The estimate uses the biblical age at accession and the usual reconstruction of his reign. Chronologies differ by a few years.
ahaz.importance: Ahaz faces invasion by Aram and Israel. Isaiah tells him to trust God, but Ahaz seeks Assyrian help. His choice brings Judah under stronger Assyrian control.
ahaz.connections: Son of Jotham. Father of Hezekiah. Opponent of Rezin and Pekah. Member of the royal house of David.

pekah.name: Pekah
pekah.dateNote: His death near 732 BCE is well placed in the regional chronology. The length and dates of his rule remain disputed.
pekah.importance: Pekah joins Rezin against Judah. This Syro-Ephraimite crisis forms the setting for Isaiah’s counsel to Ahaz and for the Immanuel prophecy.
pekah.connections: Ally of Rezin. Enemy of Ahaz. Son of Remaliah.

remaliah.name: Remaliah
remaliah.life: Years of birth and death unknown; lived in the eighth century BCE
remaliah.dateNote: Isaiah identifies Pekah as the son of Remaliah but gives no dates or other biographical details for Remaliah.
remaliah.importance: Isaiah repeatedly uses Remaliah’s name to identify Pekah during the war against Judah. The text does not present Remaliah as a participant in that war.

uzziah.name: Uzziah
uzziah.role: King of Judah, also called Azariah
uzziah.dateNote: The estimate uses the biblical age and length of reign. Proposed regnal chronologies differ because they include periods of shared rule.
uzziah.importance: Isaiah dates his call vision to the year of Uzziah’s death. That transition closes a long reign and introduces a period of political danger.
uzziah.connections: Father of Jotham. Grandfather of Ahaz. Great-grandfather of Hezekiah.

jotham.name: Jotham
jotham.dateNote: The estimate uses the biblical age at accession. Shared rule with Uzziah and Ahaz makes exact dates uncertain.
jotham.importance: Jotham’s reign belongs to the opening historical frame of Isaiah. The pressures that dominate the time of Ahaz grew during his later years.
jotham.connections: Son of Uzziah. Father of Ahaz. Grandfather of Hezekiah.

david.name: David
david.role: King of Israel and founder of Judah’s royal dynasty
david.dateNote: These are traditional historical estimates. The sources do not give dates in the modern calendar.
david.importance: David lived centuries before Isaiah, but his royal house shapes the book’s promises and warnings. Isaiah links future just rule with David’s family line.
david.connections: Ancestor of Ahaz and Hezekiah. His father was Jesse. Jerusalem became his capital.

jesse.name: Jesse
jesse.life: Years of birth and death unknown; lived about the eleventh century BCE
jesse.dateNote: The biblical accounts place Jesse one generation before David. They do not give calendar dates for his life.
jesse.importance: Isaiah uses a shoot from Jesse’s family line as an image of a future ruler. The image recalls David’s origins and renews hope for his royal house.
jesse.connections: Father of David. Ancestor of Ahaz and Hezekiah.

amoz.name: Amoz
amoz.life: Years of birth and death unknown; lived in the eighth century BCE
amoz.dateNote: The book identifies Isaiah as the son of Amoz but gives no other certain biographical details. Amoz is not the prophet Amos.
amoz.importance: Amoz identifies Isaiah’s family line throughout the book. Claims that he belonged to Judah’s royal family are later traditions, not facts stated in Isaiah.

shear-jashub.name: Shear-jashub
shear-jashub.role: Son of Isaiah whose name means “a remnant will return”
shear-jashub.dateNote: Isaiah 7 places him with his father during the reign of Ahaz. The text gives no birth or death year.
shear-jashub.importance: God tells Isaiah to take Shear-jashub when he meets Ahaz. His symbolic name introduces the book’s remnant theme during a national crisis.
shear-jashub.connections: Son of Isaiah. Brother of Maher-shalal-hash-baz. Present when Isaiah meets Ahaz.

maher-shalal-hash-baz.name: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
maher-shalal-hash-baz.role: Son of Isaiah with a prophetic symbolic name
maher-shalal-hash-baz.life: Born about 734 BCE; death year unknown
maher-shalal-hash-baz.dateNote: The birth estimate follows the setting of the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. Isaiah gives no later biography or death date.
maher-shalal-hash-baz.importance: His name means that spoil and prey will come quickly. Isaiah connects the child’s early years with the approaching Assyrian defeat of Damascus and Samaria.
maher-shalal-hash-baz.connections: Son of Isaiah. Brother of Shear-jashub. His birth sign concerns Rezin and Pekah.

isaiah.name: Isaiah
isaiah.dateNote: His exact birth and death years are unknown. Isaiah 1:1 places his work during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.
isaiah.importance: Isaiah is the central prophetic voice of the book. He warns Judah about injustice and misplaced trust. He also gives hope through the themes of a remnant, a faithful king, restoration, and God’s rule over the nations.
isaiah.connections: Son of Amoz. Counselor to Ahaz and Hezekiah. Father of Shear-jashub and Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The book records his words, signs, and visions.

hezekiah.name: Hezekiah
hezekiah.dateNote: The estimate follows a common chronology. Proposed dates vary because the biblical regnal data can include shared rule.
hezekiah.importance: Hezekiah is the king at the center of the Assyrian crisis of 701 BCE. He seeks Isaiah’s counsel, prays during the siege, recovers from illness, and later receives Babylonian envoys.
hezekiah.connections: Son of Ahaz. Adversary of Sennacherib. Advised by Isaiah. Host to the envoys of Merodach-baladan.

sennacherib.name: Sennacherib
sennacherib.dateNote: His death in 681 BCE is secure. His birth year is an estimate.
sennacherib.importance: Sennacherib invades Judah in 701 BCE and takes many fortified towns. Jerusalem survives. Isaiah 36–37 presents the crisis as a test of trust in God rather than imperial power.
sennacherib.connections: Enemy of Hezekiah. King served by the Rabshakeh. Son of Sargon II. Father of Esarhaddon.

sargon-ii.name: Sargon II
sargon-ii.dateNote: Assyrian records securely place his reign from 722 to 705 BCE. His birth year is approximate.
sargon-ii.importance: Isaiah dates the sign concerning Egypt and Cush to Sargon’s campaign against Ashdod. This is the only place where the Bible names Sargon II.
sargon-ii.connections: Father and predecessor of Sennacherib. Assyrian ruler during part of Isaiah’s ministry.

esarhaddon.name: Esarhaddon
esarhaddon.dateNote: Assyrian records place his reign from 681 to 669 BCE. His birth year is approximate.
esarhaddon.importance: Isaiah names Esarhaddon as Sennacherib’s successor after the king’s assassination. His accession closes the long historical span within Isaiah 37.

rabshakeh.name: The Rabshakeh
rabshakeh.role: Senior Assyrian official and royal spokesman
rabshakeh.life: Years of birth and death unknown; active in 701 BCE
rabshakeh.dateNote: Rabshakeh is a title, not a personal name. The text does not identify this official’s name or lifespan.
rabshakeh.importance: The Rabshakeh delivers Sennacherib’s challenge at Jerusalem. His speech attacks trust in Egypt, Hezekiah, and the Lord. It sets up the central question of Isaiah 36–37: whom will Judah trust?
rabshakeh.connections: Representative of Sennacherib. Speaks with Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah before Jerusalem’s people.

eliakim.name: Eliakim
eliakim.life: Years of birth and death unknown; active in the late eighth century BCE
eliakim.dateNote: Isaiah places Eliakim in office during Hezekiah’s reign. No exact lifespan is known.
eliakim.importance: Eliakim receives authority over the royal household and later represents Hezekiah during the Assyrian confrontation. He helps carry the crisis report to Isaiah.
eliakim.connections: Colleague of Shebna and Joah. Servant of Hezekiah.

shebna.name: Shebna
shebna.role: Royal official and scribe in Judah
shebna.life: Years of birth and death unknown; active in the late eighth century BCE
shebna.dateNote: The text records his offices during Hezekiah’s time but does not give his lifespan.
shebna.importance: Isaiah rebukes Shebna’s pride in chapter 22. Later, Shebna serves as a scribe in the delegation that hears the Assyrian demand.
shebna.connections: Colleague of Eliakim and Joah. Official under Hezekiah.

joah.name: Joah
joah.life: Years of birth and death unknown; active in 701 BCE
joah.dateNote: Isaiah identifies his office and father but gives no lifespan.
joah.importance: Joah joins Eliakim and Shebna in the delegation that hears the Rabshakeh. He helps report the Assyrian message to Hezekiah.
joah.connections: Colleague of Eliakim and Shebna. Servant of Hezekiah.

merodach-baladan.name: Merodach-baladan
merodach-baladan.role: Babylonian king, also called Marduk-apla-iddina II
merodach-baladan.dateNote: His final years are not fully clear. Historical reconstructions usually place his death around 694 BCE.
merodach-baladan.importance: He sends envoys to Hezekiah. Their visit looks friendly, but Isaiah uses it to point toward a later Babylonian removal of Judah’s wealth and royal descendants.
merodach-baladan.connections: Rival of Assyria. Sender of the embassy to Hezekiah. Contemporary of Sennacherib.

nebuchadnezzar.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
nebuchadnezzar.dateNote: The birth year is approximate. Babylonian records place his reign from 605 to 562 BCE.
nebuchadnezzar.importance: Nebuchadnezzar lived after Isaiah’s eighth-century setting. His armies captured Jerusalem and destroyed the city in 586 BCE. These events form the exile setting anticipated in Isaiah 39 and addressed by later parts of the book.
nebuchadnezzar.connections: Son of Nabopolassar. Babylonian conqueror of Judah. Predecessor in the empire later conquered by Cyrus.

nabopolassar.name: Nabopolassar
nabopolassar.dateNote: Babylonian records place his reign from 626 to 605 BCE. His birth year is unknown.
nabopolassar.importance: Nabopolassar helped end Assyrian rule and established the Babylonian dynasty that later conquered Judah. He lived after Isaiah’s eighth-century setting.
nabopolassar.connections: Father and predecessor of Nebuchadnezzar II.

cyrus.name: Cyrus II
cyrus.dateNote: Ancient sources do not give a certain birth year. His death is usually dated to 530 BCE.
cyrus.importance: Isaiah names Cyrus as the ruler who will defeat Babylon and permit restoration. The book calls him God’s anointed, although he is a foreign king.
cyrus.connections: Conqueror of Babylon in 539 BCE. Ruler associated with the return of displaced peoples and the rebuilding of temples.
